<reason>Both sides were sharp and well-disciplined, and the debate narrowed cleanly to one crux: does changing title change anything if extraction can continue under public contract? CON exploited PRO's concession brilliantly ("a change of deed is not a change of hydrology"), which forced PRO to abandon the softer Flint/incentive line. But PRO's answer to that pressure was the strongest single mechanism in the debate: ownership reallocates the burden of proof and litigation default — revoking a permit requires an agency to prove causation and drawdown against a well-lawyered counterparty, while declining to renew a supply contract requires no record at all. CON's rejoinder depended on stipulating an ideally drafted instrument (seasonal, cuttable, no dry-year volume), which PRO then turned effectively: who drafts it, and why did Michigan/Inland Empire/Maharashtra keep producing the wet-year giveaway? "Bad government, not private title" and "a supply contract is a property interest with the serial numbers filed off" were CON's best replies, but they were asserted more than developed. CON does leave one genuinely unanswered cost — the ban's reach over groundwater under private parcels — and the trade-ban point was answered only late and thinly ("bottlers don't have to buy, they have to be allowed to"), which reads as theoretical rather than actual. PRO's closing gave the cleaner decision rule ("who has to be right in advance? who eats the uncertainty?"), making the vote easier to cast. Clear but competitive.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's A1/A2 in Rebuttal 2: converting CON's "deed doesn't change hydrology" hit into a burden-of-proof asymmetry — revocation requires proving causation in court, nonrenewal requires nothing — which forced CON to retreat to a hypothetically perfect permit, the very drafting failure PRO had already shown recurring across three jurisdictions.</best_rebuttal>
